points: The chapter's message: it is not only what you do, it is where you do it. Yechezkel lists the sins behind the churban - murder, dishonoring parents, oppressing the widow and orphan, desecrating sanctified food, Shabbos violation, lashon hara, immorality, bribery, interest. All of them appear together in one place in the Torah: parshas Kedoshim.

The second section compares the people to impure metals thrown into a fire to burn away the dross - and Hashem says He will gather them all into Yerushalayim to burn them. The bitter irony: as the Babylonians approached, everyone from the mountains and outlying areas streamed into Yerushalayim for safety, and the city itself became the inferno.

The third section is a social breakdown: not everyone sinned, but nobody stood up to say 'this is wrong.' Those with the ability to protest did not protest. Hashem says 'lo matzasi' - I searched and found no one.

Dr. Ganzel points out that the word 'bah' - in it, in the city - appears ten times in the chapter: the severity lies in sinning in this place. Kedoshim says the land vomited out the Canaanim for these very sins, and Achashverosh's outrage at Haman captures it - attacking the queen is one thing, doing it 'while I am in the house' is worse. Eretz Yisrael is Hashem's house; a sin committed in Baltimore or New York is bad, but the same sin there is far worse.

The application, quoting the Lubavitcher Rebbe's approach to traveling to Israel: if you go, even for a week, take something special on and elevate yourself for that time. You cannot be the same person in Israel that you are at home. We have to recognize where we are - we are in God's home, and we have to act appropriately.
